sentences.text: 10.50 If a lawyer for a party engages in serious misconduct, the Court may order the lawyer to pay a costs award with respect to a person named in the order.

There is no direct appellate authority on this new rule, or the circumstances in which the rule should be engaged, although such awards are considered to be extraordinary: Quebec (Director of Criminal and Penal Prosecutions) v Jodoin, 2017 SCC 26 at para.

The interpretation of this rule, and its application in any particular situation, engages the tension between the lawyer's obligation to the client, and the lawyer's obligation to the system of justice. … 8 The respondents emphasize the highly deferential standard of review citing, for example, the statements at paras.

51–2 of Jodoin: It was not open to the Court of Appeal to intervene without first identifying an error of law, a palpable and overriding error in the motion judge's analysis of the facts, or an unreasonable or clearly wrong exercise of his discretion. … In a case involving an exercise of discretion, an appellate court must show great deference and must be cautious in intervening, doing so only where it is established that the discretion was exercised in an abusive, unreasonable or non-judicial manner … The respondents argue that no such error can be identified here, and that permission to appeal should not be granted because the decision below is “correct”.

This argument misapprehends the test for permission to appeal, as well as the role of individual appellate judges who hear applications for permission to appeal: CCS Corp. v Secure Energy Services Inc., 2017 ABCA 260 at paras.
The test for permission to appeal is whether there is a “good arguable case”, not whether the appeal is likely to succeed.

On an application for permission to appeal the point is not just whether the decision below is right or wrong, but whether the issue is important enough that a full panel of this Court should say whether it is right or wrong.
Whether there is a “good arguable case” depends in part on the merits of the appeal, and the standard of review that will be applied, but it is not an invitation to pre-decide the appeal.
In Forsyth v.
180 (Alta.
Q.B.), Acton J. set out the following test for granting leave to appeal an order for costs (at p.
181): 2 The Alberta Court of Appeal has determined in Colburn Capital Corporation v.
54277 Alberta Ltd., [1999] 8 W.W.R.
222, that there is a four-part test for granting leave to appeal an order for costs.
3 The Applicant must establish that:
(a) there is a good, arguable case having enough merit to warrant scrutiny by the Court [of Appeal]
(b) the issues are important, both in general, and to the parties
(c) the appeal has some practical utility, and
(d) there will not be an unreasonable delay caused by the proceedings.
In Serfas v.

Spady, 2024 ABCA 314, Justice Wakeling gave this summary of test for granting permission to appeal a costs award: [2] The test for granting permission to appeal a costs award has two distinct dimensions – each of which is onerous.

[3] The first dimension requires the applicant to satisfy the court that the error attributed to the decision-maker is a question of law that is of general important to the practice, that the applicant's prospects of success approach the more-likely-than-not point on the scale and that an appeal will not hinder the progress of the action.
[4] The second stream does not focus on legal error.
Instead, the applicant must establish that the court's order is clearly wrong and, under all the circumstances, must be set aside.
This concept recognizes that a decision-maker can correctly state the law but apply it in a manner that is indefensible.
[5] Costs awards seldom turn on issues that have not arisen before and, as a result, are rarely the subject of a permission to appeal order.
As Justice Feehan opined, “[p]ermission to appeal costs should be granted only rarely”.
[Footnotes omitted] Also see, “Leave”, supra.
Test also applies to “public-interest advance-costs orders” In Anderson v.
Alberta, 2020 ABCA 22, 2020 CarswellAlta 106, Her Majesty the Queen in Right of Alberta sought leave to appeal a “public-interest advance-costs order” issued against the Crown and in favour of Ms.
Anderson and the Beaver Lake Cree Nation.
The order required the Crown to pay $300,000 annually toward Beaver Lake's legal fees for the duration of the litigation.
Wakeling, J.A., in granting leave, said: [10] This Court has frequently stated that an applicant seeking to appeal a costs award must pass a multi-part test.
There is no good reason not to apply the same standard to public-interest advance-costs orders, a subset of costs awards.
The test is the one set out above.
Amount in Controversy The plaintiff now appeals from that judgment, pursuant to the Yukon Act, RSC, 1952, ch.
53, sec.

35 [2]) whereby an appeal is given to this court from any final judgment of the Territorial Court, “where the matter in controversy amounts to the sum or value of five hundred dollars or upwards.” The proper measure of value for determining the right of appeal to the Judicial Committee is defined by the Earl of Selborne, speaking for their Lordships' board in Allan v.
Pratt

(1888), 13 App Cas 780, 57 LJPC 104, as “the amount which has been recovered by the plaintiff in the action, and against which the appeal could be brought.”“Their Lordships *** would agree in principle with the rule laid down in the judgment of this tribunal delivered by Lord Chelmsford in Macfarlane v.

Leclaire (1862), 15 Moo PC 181 … that is, that the judgment is to be looked at as it affects the interests of the party who is prejudiced by it, and who seeks to relieve himself from it by appeal;”… In my opinion sec.
80 of the Yukon Act is in substance and effect analogous to the legislation under consideration in the foregoing decisions.

Therefore, upon the application of the principles laid down in those decisions, I think there can be no doubt that this appeal is incompetent, since the appellant seeks to have set aside a judgment against him of only $300.
The matter in controversy, therefore, as the judgment affects the interest of the appellant, amounts to no more than $300.
In my view the appeal must therefore be dismissed for want of jurisdiction in this court to entertain it.
Warrington v.
Whitehorse Hotels Ltd.
In Jackson v.
Alberta Social Housing Corp., 2011 ABCA 232, 2011 CarswellAlta 1315, Slatter, J.A. discussed how to determine the value of “the matter in controversy” as referred to in R.

In the case before him the facts (as set out in paragraph 2) were as follows: 2 The appellants sued the respondent claiming entitlement to real estate commissions of approximately $870,000 based on a percentage of the value of the property.
The trial judge awarded only $13,480 after finding that the appellants were only entitled to an hourly rate, not a percentage commission, and the appellants now appeal the quantum.
The respondents on the proposed appeal contended that leave to appeal under R.
505(4) was required.

His Lordship disagreed, and said, at paragraphs 4–6: 4 The amount in controversy is determined by the effect that the judgment under appeal would have on the interests of the person proposing to appeal: Macfarlane v.
Leclaire (1862), 15 Moo.
P.C.
In this appeal the appellants do not seek a sum of less than $25,000.
What they are seeking is the difference between their original claim of $870,000, and what the trial judge awarded, which is well in excess of the monetary limit.
The “matter in controversy in the appeal” is the difference between the two amounts, not the $13,480.
5 This is not a case like Hogan v.
Canada, [1977] 1 S.C.R.
413, 66 D.L.R (3d) 571 where the amount allegedly in issue on the appeal depended on the bare allegation of the appellant.
Here the argument about the commissions being based on a percentage is an arguable one on the record.
It is also not a case like Kennett v.
Superior Millwork Ltd., 2004 ABCA 56, 54 Alta.
L.R.
104 or Warrington v.
Whitehorse Hotels Ltd.
(N.S.) 200 (B.C.C.A.) where the difference between the amount claimed and the amount recovered at trial was less than the monetary limit.
6 On the other hand, if the respondent had appealed the judgment of $13,480, then leave would have been required.
Leave to Appeal Security for Costs order In Thompson v.
International Union of Operating Engineers Local No.

995, 2017 ABCA 193, 2017 CarswellAlta 1039, Madam Justice Schutz set out the test for leave to appeal a security for costs order: 13 Obtaining permission, or leave, to appeal an order for security for costs is subject to a high threshold.
Permission to appeal will only be granted if the appeal raises a serious question of general importance and has a reasonable chance of success.

Whether a procedural appeal has a reasonable chance of success is assessed by determining whether the chambers judge erred in law, unreasonably exercised a discretion, or misapprehended an important fact: Autoweld Systems Limited v CRC-Evans Pipeline International, Inc., 2011 ABCA 243 at para 8, 515 AR 6; see also Jeerh v Yorkton Securities Inc., 2005 ABCA 64 (CanLII) at paras 25–27, 363 AR 333
Liu v Tangirala, 2005 ABCA 299 (CanLII) at paras 6-7, 380 AR 172.

14 A strong measure of deference on appeal is owed to a decision by a case management judge concerning security for costs, as case management judges are entitled to consider whether, in light of the history to date, a given suit should occupy further court time and if so, on what conditions: Noscenco v Bagayeva, 2016 ABCA 242 at paras 15–22.
15 Given that leave to appeal a security for costs order is subject to a high threshold, leave should rarely be granted: Grabowski v Bodnar, 2007 ABCA 280 at para 7, 429 AR 1.

The application should be heard by a different judge Rules 14.5(1)(a) and 14.5(2) require before one may appeal the order of a single judge of the Court of Appeal, one needs the leave of that judge to appeal.
In Prefontaine v.
Minister of National Revenue (2001), 97 Alta.
L.R.

(3d) 37 (C.A.), Berger J.A. held that Rule 505(6) (the predecessor to Rules 14.5(1)(a) and 14.5(2)) raised constitutional concerns, and that a judge other than the one who granted the order should hear the application for leave to appeal from it.
At pp.
39–40, His Lordship said: Rule 505(6), however, does require that the judge decide whether or not his judgment should be reviewed.

I respectfully agree with the Federal Court of Appeal that the question “should my judgment be appealed?” is “an entirely different question” from “does this case raise a serious issue of general importance?” There is no common law right of appeal, but when the Legislature chooses to provide a mechanism for appeal, that mechanism, in my opinion, must function in a manner that respects the principles of natural justice.
I have concluded that Rule 505(6) places the Appellants' s.
7 [Charter] rights in jeopardy and offends the principles of fundamental justice.

Notwithstanding the presumption of neutrality and the significance of the oath of office taken by judges, a reasonable person properly informed would apprehend bias on the part of a judge called upon to decide whether his judgment should be appealed.
The motion for leave to appeal must be heard by another judge of the Court.
Berger J.A.'s comments were the subject of some comment with some judges worrying that his Lordship had pronounced on constitutional validity which was beyond his mandate in the circumstances.
In Liu v.
Tangirala (2005), 371 A.R.
71 (C.A.), at pp.
72–74, Berger J.A. clarified his position: In Prefontaine v.
Minister of National Revenue (2001), 293 A.R 369, 257 W.A.C.
369 (C.A.), I recused myself from an application for leave to appeal to a three person panel an order which I had given in chambers.
In the circumstances of that case, I cited various concerns regarding the potential effect of Rule 505(6) on the rights of the parties.
I stated: … Rule 505(6) places the Appellants' s.
7 rights in jeopardy and offends the principles of fundamental justice.

Notwithstanding the presumption of neutrality and the significance of the oath of office taken by judges, a reasonable person properly informed would apprehend bias on the part of a judge called upon to decide whether his judgment should be appealed.
The motion for leave to appeal must be heard by another judge of the Court. … (Prefontaine at para.
7) Those observations have attracted a measure of criticism.
By way of illustration, Fruman, J.A., in Vysek v.
Nova Gas International Ltd. et al., [2002] A.J.
No.
209 (C.A.) (“Vysek No.

1”), was of the opinion that my decision “is troubling from a jurisdictional perspective.” She opined: … a constitutional challenge to legislation must be brought before a judge who has jurisdiction to decide it, and certain procedural requirements must be met.
A challenge to legislation that is based on a violation of the rules of natural justice is also a constitutional challenge because s.
7 of the Charter‘constitutionally enshrines principles of natural justice and procedural fairness’: R. v.
Langevin (1984), 8 D.L.R.
With great respect, Fruman, J.A., has mischaracterized the issue in Prefontaine, supra.
No constitutional challenge to legislation was brought; no constitutional questions were posed; no declaration of constitutional invalidity was pronounced.
The sole issue was recusal.
The issue was also taken up by Hunt, J.A., in Vysek v.
Nova Gas Intl.
No.
221 (C.A.) (“Vysek No.
She took note of Fruman, J.A.'s, judgment in Vysek No.
1 but recognized that the reasons for decision in Prefontaine merely “expressed the view that Rule 505(6) potentially breached an appellant's s.
7 Charter rights and offended the principles of fundamental justice because it required a judge to determine whether or not his own judgment should be appealed.” (at para.
30 of Vysek No.

2) (emphasis added) Hunt, J.A., seems to have understood that the reference in Prefontaine to Rule 505(6) placing the Appellants'“rights in jeopardy” scarcely equates with a formal pronouncement that rights had been or would necessarily be violated.
Hunt, J.A., is right.
No constitutional infringement was found in Prefontaine.
Fruman, J.A., was, with respect, in error in so concluding.
She failed to recognize the distinction between a judge's concern for “potential breach” in the context of recusal and a finding of constitutional invalidity.
A constitutional challenge to legislation must, of course, be brought in a Court that has jurisdiction to decide it.
In Vysek No.
1, the applicants “challenge[d] the constitutionality of the leave requirement, arguing that it offends s.
7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the principles of fundamental justice.” (at para.
1) [see footnote 1].
Fruman, J.A., acknowledged that a single Court of Appeal judge in chambers “does not have authority to pronounce R.
505(6), or any other legislation, unconstitutional or contrary to the principles of fundamental justice.” (at para.
20) [see footnote 2].
I agree.
Whether Rule 505(6) infringes the principles of fundamental justice or does not is beyond the jurisdictional competence of a single appellate judge.
Yet, in Vysek No.
1, Fruman, J.A., did not hesitate to declare that Rule 505(6) does not offend the principles of fundamental justice.
With great respect, that decision “is troubling from a jurisdictional perspective.” With all of the foregoing in mind, I turn to the present application for leave to appeal to a three person panel.
In my reasons issued on May 17, 2005 (dismissing the initial application) I said in part: On this record, I am persuaded that the Applicant does not have a reasonable chance of success on appeal.

The Applicant has failed to establish on a standard of arguable merit that the case management judge ‘did not give sufficient weight to relevant factors, proceeded arbitrarily or on an erroneous view of the facts, or that the order would result in a failure of justice’ (Armstrong v.
Shapiro, [2005] A.J.
No.
Nor am I persuaded that the appeal of the discretionary procedural direction in this case raises an important question of law or a precedent of importance to the parties.

Mindful of the pronouncement of “no arguable merit” and “no reasonable chance of success on appeal”, a reasonable, fair-minded and informed person, viewing the matter realistically and practically, and having thought the matter through, would apprehend bias on the part of a judge who so opined and who is then called upon to decide whether leave to appeal to a three person panel should be allowed.

With great respect to Fruman, J.A., this is very different from the contention (which we both agree is mistaken) “that judicial continuity gives rise to an apprehension of bias or that losing a motion before a judge entitles a litigant to forever after be free of that judge, whether in other law suits, later motions in the same suit, or motions to rehear or reconsider previous rulings: Broda v.
120 at 123 (C.A.).” (Vysek No.
1 at para.
22) [see footnote 3].
As in Prefontaine, I have come to the conclusion that I must recuse myself and that the motion for leave to appeal to a three person panel must be heard by another judge of the Court.
As in Prefontaine, I express my concern that to do otherwise may place the Applicant's rights in jeopardy contrary to the principles of fundamental justice.
As in Prefontaine, I make no pronouncement of constitutional invalidity.
In Stacey v.
Foy, 2014 ABCA 447, 2014 CarswellAlta 2339, Mr.
Justice Berger reiterated the view he had expressed in Prefontaine v.
Minister of National Revenue, supra, and held that it applied to Rules 14.5(1)(a) and 14.5(2).
Test for Granting Leave In Ouellette et al v.

Law Society of Alberta, 2021 ABCA 283, 2021 CarswellAlta 1880, Justice Wakeling said [footnotes omitted]: [13] As a general rule, judicial resources should not be allocated to the review of matters assigned to single judges.

The fact that rules 14.5(2) and 14.5(3) of the Alberta Rules of Court stipulate that a party who wishes to appeal a decision of a single judge must secure the permission of the judge whose decision the party wishes to appeal and denies any right to appeal a decision of a single judge granting or denying permission to appeal confirms the existence of this policy decision—no more judges than is absolutely necessary should review a matter for which original jurisdiction is assigned to a single judge.

[14] To ensure that panels of this Court rarely review orders of single judges of the Court, a single judge of the Court of Appeal should grant permission to appeal a decision of his or hers to a panel of the Court only if there is a compelling reason to require the applicant and the respondent to reargue and three judges of the Court of Appeal to decide an issue.

[15] A compelling reason exists if the issue is of general importance to the community or of sufficient importance to the parties to justify the allocation of private resources—the parties' legal costs—and public resources—assigning three more judges to hear an appeal—associated with an appeal.
[16] The community interest portion of the test is engaged if the issue presents a legal question the answer to which will be of precedential value in the area of the law engaged.
A determination has the potential to affect the interests of others besides the disputants.
In these cases, the interests at stake are important enough to justify the investment of more resources—the attention of three more judges to a file—to resolve the controversy.
[17] Most of the issues for which a single appeal judge is responsible are settled and not controversial.
As a result, questions of this nature infrequently arise.

[18] A single appeal judge considering whether the issue is of sufficient importance to the parties may grant permission to appeal an earlier decision of his or hers if that decision is the product of a misunderstanding of the law or a misapprehension of the evidence or both and these conditions substantially contributed to the decision the applicant seeks permission to appeal.
[19] In addition, the adjudicator must be satisfied that the proposed appeal has a reasonable chance of success.
In the context of permission-to-appeal applications under rule 14.5(1)(a), a proposed appeal has a reasonable chance of success if the likelihood the appeal will succeed exceeds forty percent.
In other words, the applicant's likelihood of success must not be substantially less than the respondent's likelihood of success.

This Court would not be a careful steward of the resources the state invests in the administration of justice if it granted leave to appeal to applicants whose prospects of success were substantially less than the respondent's prospects of success.
A marked disparity in the strength of the parties' positions is a clear signal that granting leave to appeal is an imprudent order.
In Oomen v.
Capital Region Housing Corporation, 2017 ABCA 360, 2017 CarswellAlta 2140, Justice Crighton said: 1 M.G.

CRIGHTON J.A.:—This is an application pursuant to rule 14.5(1)(a) of the Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 124/2010 for permission to appeal my decision reported at 2017 ABCA 265 to a full panel of this court. … … 8 To succeed in his application, the applicant must demonstrate there is: a) a question of general importance; b) a possible error of law; c) an unreasonable exercise of discretion; or d) a misapprehension of important facts: Settlement Lenders Inc. v Blicharz 2016 ABCA 109 at para 1, leave to appeal denied, [2016] SCCA No.

275 (QL). … 10 Like applications to extend time, it is also important to consider other factors such as the proposed appeal's chance of success, the standard of appellate review and any ensuing delay: Alberta Treasury Branches v Conserve Oil 1st Corporation, 2016 ABCA 213 at para 3 citing Carbone v Whidden, 2015 ABCA 177 at para 27 and James v Northern Lakes College, 2014 ABCA 48 at para 2, 569 AR 122.
In Clark v.

Pezzente, 2017 ABCA 403, 2017 CarswellAlta 2516, Justice Veldhuis said: 5 To obtain permission to appeal from the decision of a single appeal justice, the applicant must show why a further appeal is in the interest of justice.
Relevant considerations include whether
(a) the appeal raises a question of general importance
(b) there was an arguable error of law
(c) there was an arguably unreasonable exercise of discretion, or
(d) there was an apparent misapprehension of an important fact: Alberta Health Services v Wang, 2017 ABCA 261 at paras 5–6; Oommen v Capital Region Housing Corporation, 2017 ABCA 360 at para 8.
In Moses v.
Weninger (2006), 55 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 37 (C.A.), Hunt J.A. discussed the test to be used when determining whether or not to grant leave to appeal.
At p.
42, her Ladyship said: Absent a question of general public importance, it is my view that the test governing an application under Rule 505(6) is whether
(i) there is a possible error of law
(ii) a discretion has been unreasonably exercised; or
(iii) the chambers judge misapprehended important facts.
She also said that (at p.
42): It is also worthwhile to consider the nature of the decision in regard to which leave is sought.
Stays and security for costs orders are both exercises of discretion.
Absent an error of law, reasonableness is the applicable standard in reviewing an exercise of discretion: Decock v.
Alberta, 255 A.R.
234…, at para.
13 (Alta.
In Huang v.

Canadian Western Trust, 2011 ABCA 140, 2011 CarswellAlta 731, Justice Hunt said, at paragraph 4: 4 Leave to appeal the decision of a single judge pursuant to Rule 505(6) of the Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 390/68 will be granted if the applicant can establish there is a serious question of general importance: Vysek v Nova Gas International Ltd, 2002 ABCA 112, 303 AR 209 at para 26.

Absent such a question, the test is whether there is a possible error of law; discretion has been unreasonably exercised; or the chambers judge misapprehended important facts: Moses v Weninger, 2006 ABCA 52, 380 AR 230 at para 13.
The standard of review that would be applied on an appeal is also a relevant consideration: ibid at para 12.
In Wong v.
Giannacopoulos, 2011 ABCA 277, 2011 CarswellAlta 1770, 515 A.R.

58, Justice Slatter set out the test for granting leave (at paragraph 4): 4 The most important consideration in granting leave to appeal is whether the proposed appeal raises a serious issue of general importance with a reasonable chance of success.

Other factors include: whether there is a possible error of law; whether a discretion has been unreasonably exercised; whether the chambers judge misapprehended important facts; whether there are conflicting decisions on the point; the standard of review that would be applied on the appeal; and whether there are other good reasons why a full panel of the Court should review the order under appeal: Vysek v.
Nova Gas International Ltd., 2002 ABCA 112, 4 Alta LR (4th) 287, 303 AR 209 at paras.
33-34; Vysek v.
Nova Gas International Ltd., 2002 ABCA 136, 303 AR 221 at paras.
13–7; Moses v.
Weninger, 2006 ABCA 52, 55 Alta LR (4th) 37, 380 AR 230 at paras.
10–13; Dhala v.
Dhala, 2008 ABCA 259 at para.
In Al-Ghamdi v.

Alberta, 2017 ABCA 255, 2017 CarswellAlta 1363, Justice Slatter gave this summary of the factors to be considered in applications for leave to appeal: 2 The requirement for permission to appeal serves a gate-keeping function.
The applicant must demonstrate why it is in the interests of justice to have a further level of review.

A number of factors are considered in deciding whether an appeal from the decision of a single judge is appropriate: whether the proposed appeal raises a serious issue; whether there is a possible error of law; whether it is arguable that a discretion has been unreasonably exercised; whether the single judge misapprehended important facts; whether there are conflicting decisions on the point; the standard of review that would be applied on the appeal; and whether there are other good reasons why a full panel of the Court should review the order under appeal: Wong v Giannacopoulos, 2011 ABCA 277 at para.
4, 515 AR 58; James v Northern Lakes College, 2014 ABCA 48 at para.
2, 569 AR 122; Schulte v Alberta (Workers' Compensation Board), 2015 ABCA 268 at para.
3 An important consideration is whether the applicant has identified a serious issue justifying another level of review.
Assessment of the seriousness of the issue involves consideration of a number of factors: • the perceived strength of the argument.
The applicant need not show that he is likely to be successful, but he must demonstrate more than that the appeal is not frivolous.
The Court must be satisfied that the issue has a reasonable chance of success; • the importance of the issue to the parties; and • the general importance of the issue within the larger legal system.
Merely wanting to reargue the same matters is not sufficient.
See also (to the same effect): Stanfield v.
Low, 2019 ABCA 219, 2019 CarswellAlta 1090 at paragraphs 3–4.
In Kindylides v.

Korol, 2012 ABCA 195, 2012 CarswellAlta 1065, Madam Justice Picard said, at paragraph 2: 2 The test governing applications under Rule 505(6) was set out by Ritter J.A. in DataNet Information Systems, Inc. v.
Belzil, 2011 ABCA 40 at para.
2, leave to appeal to the SCC refused, [2011] S.C.C.A.
No.

163, 34196 (September 29, 2011): The applicable rule for this form of relief, Rule 505(6), has been interpreted to state that a justice should grant leave to appeal if the issues engage a serious question of general importance, or, absent such a question, if there is a possible error of law, a discretion has been unreasonably exercised, or the initial decision was based on a misapprehension of important facts: Vysek v.
Nova Gas International Ltd., 2002 ABCA 136, 303 A.R.
221 at para.
16; Moses v.
Weninger, 2006 ABCA 52, 380 A.R.
230 at para.
In Shaw v.

Belcourt, 2011 ABCA 183, 2011 CarswellAlta 977, Watson, J.A. at paragraphs 3 and 6, explained the test to a self represented party: 3. … in order to take an application from a single judge to a panel of this court, there is a policy that leave to appeal a judgment of the court that is given by a single judge to a panel will be granted if the applicant can establish that there is a serious question of general importance that is to be taken to the panel and in the absence of such a question, the test then comes down to whether or not the judgment made by the single judge is reviewable within the standards provided for by the law. … 6. … you would have to show that there was an error of law on my part or you would have to show that my discretion to turn down your applications was unreasonably exercised or you would have to show that I misapprehended important facts about the matter.
In Schulte v.

Alberta (Appeals Commission for Workers' Compensation Board), 2015 ABCA 268, Madam Justice Veldhuis set out the test for granting leave to appeal the decision of a single appellate judge: 6 Permission to appeal the decision of a single appellate justice will be granted only on the following basis: 1.
A serious question of general importance; 2.
A possible error of law; 3.
Unreasonable exercise of discretion; or 4.
Misapprehension of important facts: Moses v Weninger, 2006 ABCA 52 at para 13, 380 AR 230; JH Drilling Inc v Alberta (Natural Resources Conservation Board), 2014 ABCA 312 at para 5, 580 AR 386.
7 This Court has described a serious question as that which involves an appeal that is not frivolous, but rather one that has a reasonable chance of success.
A general question of importance involves a matter of policy, principle or law that might have precedential value.
It requires more than a disagreement with a factual interpretation or quarrel with an exercise of discretion: Vysek v Nova Gas International Ltd, 2002 ABCA 112 at para 34, 303 AR 209.
To the same effect, see: Alberta Health Services v.
Wang, 2017 ABCA 261, 2017 CarswellAlta 1433, 58 Alta.
L.R.
(6th) 109 at paragraphs 4–6.
In Attila Dogan Construction and Installation Co. v.

AMEC Americas Ltd., 2015 ABCA 257, Justice Slatter said: 2 The respondents argue that the issue should be reconsidered by a full panel of this Court, because other decisions of single appeal judges on the test for extending the time to appeal are inconsistent.
That sort of inconsistency is one potential basis for granting permission to appeal a single-judge decision to the Court: Koska v Alberta (Treasury Branches), 2002 ABCA 138 at para.
42, 4 Alta LR (4th) 73, 303 AR 230; R. v Hubek, 2011 ABCA 86 at para.
6; Wong v Giannacopoulos, 2011 ABCA 277 at para.
Justice Slatter did not grant leave in that case.
In Hayden v.
Smith, 2017 ABCA 62, 2017 CarswellAlta 231, Justice Rowbotham gave this summary of the law: 5 An application for permission to appeal a decision of a single appellate judge is not a rehearing.
Permission will be granted on a serious question of general importance: Vysek v Nova Gas International Ltd, 2002 ABCA 112, 303 AR 209.

Absent such a question the applicant must demonstrate an error of law, jurisdiction or principle (Carbone v Whidden, 2015 ABCA 177 at para 27); that discretion was exercised unreasonably; or, that the initial decision was based on a misapprehension of important facts: Alberta Treasury Branches v Conserve Oil 1st Corporation, 2016 ABCA 213 at para 3.

Other factors are the proposed appeal's chance of success, the standard of appellate review and the ensuing delay: Alberta Treasury Branches at para 3, citing Carbonne at paras 28–33; see also Park Avenue Flooring Inc v EllisDon Construction Services Inc., 2016 ABCA 327.
6 My role under Rule 14.5(1)(a) is one of gate keeper.
When an application has been denied by a single judge, the court must be persuaded that the issue warrants the attention of three members of this court. … In SRG Takamiya Co.
Ltd. v.

58376 Alberta Ltd., 2019 ABCA 301, 2019 CarswellAlta 1659, Justice Rowbotham spoke about how the “interests of justice” must be considered: [5] Permission can be granted if the applicant establishes that there is:
(a) a question of general importance
(b) a possible error of law
(c) an unreasonable exercise of discretion; or

(d) a misapprehension of important facts: Settlement Lenders Inc v Blicharz, 2016 ABCA 109 at para 1, leave to appeal to SCC refused, [2016] SCCA No 275 (QL), citing Schulte v Alberta (Appeals Commission for Workers' Compensation Board), 2015 ABCA 268 at para 6.

The fundamental hurdle is to show it is in the interests of justice to have a panel review the single judge's decision; hence the applicant has to show that one substantial criteria (as set out in Schulte, Blicharz and TD Auto-Finance (Canada) v Smith-Johnson, 2016 ABCA 388 at paras 4–6) is met: Al-Ghamdi v Alberta, 2016 ABCA 403 at paras 10–12.
[6] Whether it is in the interests of justice to justify another level of review includes an assessment of the seriousness of the issue.

This involves consideration of a number of factors: the perceived strength of the argument (the applicant need not show a likelihood of success, but the applicant must demonstrate more than that the appeal is not frivolous, the court must be satisfied that the issue has a reasonable chance of success); the importance of the issue to the parties; and the general importance of the issue within the larger legal system: Alberta Health Services v Wang, 2017 ABCA 261 at para 6.
Is an issue “moot”?
In The Alberta Teachers' Association v.

Buffalo Trail Public Schools Regional Division No 28, 2022 ABCA 13, 2022 CarswellAlta 92, Justice Wakeling discussed the concept of mootness (footnotes omitted): [17] The law is clear that an action or proceeding is moot if there is no “live controversy” that divides the parties and the resolution of which will actually affect the parties' rights or interests: The doctrine of mootness is an aspect of a general policy or practice that a court may decline to decide a case which raises merely a hypothetical or abstract question.
The general principle applies when the decision of the court will not have the effect of resolving some controversy which affects or may affect the rights of the parties.
If the decision of the court will have no practical effect on such rights, the court will decline to decide the case.
This essential ingredient must be present not only when the action or proceeding is commenced but at the time when the court is called upon to reach a decision.

Accordingly if, subsequent to the initiation of the action or proceeding, events occur which affect the relationship of the parties so that no present live controversy exists which affects the rights of the parties, the case is said to be moot.
[18] Most of the time it is in the public interest to remove moot cases from the litigation stream.

The judicial branch of government has finite resources and they are best expended to resolve controversies that actually affect the parties' interests and merit the expenditure of public taxpayers' funds.
A court relieved of the obligation to decide a moot case is free to decide other cases.
[19] The law governing declarations is consistent with the law governing mootness.
A court cannot make a declaration unless “it will settle a “live controversy” between the parties”.
[20] But what are the benchmarks of a “live controversy”?

[21] Is there a “live controversy” only if the parties' pleadings or other filed material or both, objectively assessed, demonstrate that there is an unresolved dispute between a party and another party adverse in interest the resolution of which will actually affect the parties' rights or interests?
[22] Suppose P files a claim against D, a statutory delegate, alleging that Bylaw 123 passed by D contravenes the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and is unconstitutional.
After D files a statement of defence denying the claim, D repeals Bylaw 123.
P subsequently files an application seeking an order compelling D to file an affidavit of records.
D opposes the application, alleging that the matter is moot.
D files an affidavit of a senior member of D stating that D has repealed Bylaw 123.
Is the claim moot because there is no longer a dispute about the validity of Bylaw 123—the bylaw does not exist anymore?
[23] Or is there a “live controversy”, as well, if the outcome is not obvious?
In other words, is there no live controversy if the position of one disputant is completely without merit and cannot possibly succeed?

[24] Suppose P files a statement of claim alleging that D cheers for the Nashville Predators in breach of his common law duty to cheer for his hometown National Hockey League team and that D's breach has caused P a compensable loss.
D files a defence in which he admits that D is a resident of Edmonton and cheers for the Nashville Predators.
D denies in his defence that his cheering for the Nashville Predators harms P in any way and that there is a common law duty to cheer for the home team.
D also asserts that the mootness doctrine applies.
D applies for an order dismissing P's action on the ground that it discloses no cause of action or is moot or both.
[25] I am not aware of a single case in which a court has applied a merit-based test to determine whether there is a “live controversy”.
Nor am I aware of any scholar who has adopted such a position.
[26] This may be a sign that the answer is so obvious that it merits no consideration.
[27] But I do not think that is the case.

[28] Assuming that the judges who constructed the “live controversy” standard intended the words to have their ordinary meaning, it will be useful to examine the dictionary meanings of “live” and “controversy”.
[29]“Live”, according to The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language”, means “[o]f current interest or relevance: a live topic; still a live option”.

Webster's Third New International Dictionary of the English Language Unabridged, offers a similar definition: “living in thought or controversy: of continuing interest: open to debate: not settled or decided”.
So does The Oxford English Dictionary: “Of questions, subjects of consideration: Of present interest and importance; not obsolete or exhausted”.
[30] These dictionaries define “controversy” much the same way.
The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language offers this definition: “A dispute, especially a public one, between sides holding opposing views”.

Webster's Third New International Dictionary of the English Language Unabridged presents this version: “a cause, occasion or instance of disagreement or contention: a difference marked esp. by the expression of opposing views”.
The Oxford English Dictionary version follows: “the contending of opponents one with another on a subject of dispute”.
[31] I conclude that a “live controversy”, in ordinary speech, does not capture settled or decided issues.
For example, the fact that members of the Flat Earth Society assert that the earth is flat does not mean that the shape of the earth is a “live controversy” today.
Scientists definitively answered this question a long time ago.
[32] This conclusion supports the notion that there is a merit-based component to “live controversy” in ordinary speech.
If the position of one of the disputants is without any merit and cannot possibly be correct, those who use the language correctly would state that there is no “live controversy”.

[33] While a reasonable person adequately conversant with the scientific literature would not characterize the issue the Flat Earth Society exists to debate as a live controversy just because of the contrarian position the Flat Earth Society adopts and would reject out of hand the assertion that the earth is flat, the law has followed a different course.
[34] I am satisfied that, for legal purposes, the mootness concept does not incorporate a merit-based component.
It is not unusual for words used by the general community in ordinary speech and by a segment of the community interested in a specific activity to have different meanings.

For lawyers and judges mootness measures only the existence—objectively assessed, based on a review of the pleadings or other filed material—of a dispute between two or more parties the resolution of which will actually affect the parties' rights or interests.

[35] The jurisprudence's sole focus on the objective assessment of the pleadings or other filed material does not limit in any way a party's ability to challenge meritless claims or a court's ability to remove meritless claims from the litigation stream.
There are other options that a litigant confronted with a hopeless or baseless claim can invoke.
A party can apply to strike out an adversary's pleading on the ground it does not disclose a cause of action or seek summary judgment.
[36] It makes no sense to expand the scope of the mootness doctrine and give it a role already assigned to other protocols each of which operates effectively and independently.
Judges should strive to simplify the law whenever possible and not, without good reason, complicate it.
In Carbone v.
Dawes 2024 ABCA 405, the plaintiff sought an order which on the face of it was moot.
Defence counsel raised “mootness”, but the chambers justice discouraged that submission and preferred to deal with the substantive matter.
The learned chambers justice then dismissed the plaintiff's application.
The plaintiff appealed that dismissal, and in the course of dealing with that appeal, the Court of Appeal said that it is the Court which will decide whether it will hear a “moot” issue.
It is not something the parties can compel by their consent.
The Court said: [7] The appellant appeals to this Court even though, because the questionings on affidavits have taken place, the substantive issue appears to be moot.
While this Court has a discretion to consider moot issues, that is not something to which the parties can consent.
Moot appeals should not generally be brought.

The consideration of moot issues consumes court resources and can involve an inappropriate exercise of the court's jurisdiction: Borowski v Canada (Attorney General), 1989 CanLII 123 (SCC), [1989] 1 SCR 342 at 360, 362, 57 DLR
(4th) 231 [Borowski].
Sometimes the discretion to hear a moot appeal will be exercised where the appeal raises an issue of public importance the resolution of which is in the public interest (Borowski at 361-362

CM v Alberta, 2024 ABCA 136 at paras 34, 37), but this medical malpractice litigation and the associated security for costs applications are private litigation involving only the interests of the parties.
R.
14.5(1)(j) – Generally In Bains v.

Adam, 2024 ABCA 271, Justice Strekaf said: [4] Rule 14.5(1)(j) of the Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 124/2010 directs that no appeal to the Court of Appeal is allowed to proceed unless permission to appeal has been obtained for “any appeal by a person who has been declared a vexatious litigant in the court appealed from.” A “vexatious litigant order” is one that “prevents a named litigant from commencing or continuing proceedings in court, unless the litigant obtains permission from the court to initiate the intended step or proceeding”: Jonsson v Lymer, 2020 ABCA 167 at para 9.

A person “has been ‘declared a vexatious litigant’ within the meaning of rule 14.5(1)(j) when they have been made subject to a vexatious litigant order, as described, whether or not the order uses the term ‘vexatious litigant’ or makes an express declaration to that effect.
The substance of the order is determinative, not the words in which it, or the reasons for it, have been expressed.”: Tican v Alamgir, 2023 ABCA 115 at para 25.
R.
14.5(1)(j)—“in the court appealed from” In Jordan v.

De Wet, 2016 ABCA 366, 2016 CarswellAlta 2225, the applicant submitted that he did not need permission to appeal because he had not been declared a vexatious litigant in the proceedings in which he sought to file an appeal.
Justice O'Ferrall disagreed.
His Lordship said, at paragraph 7: 7 Rule 14.5(1)(j) states that anyone who has been declared a vexatious litigant in the court below needs permission from the Court of Appeal to prosecute an appeal.
The words used in subrule

(j) are “in the court appealed from” not “in the action appealed from” thus indicating the rule relates to all proceedings taken or continued by the person who has been declared vexatious, including steps taken in proceedings for which permission to commence or continue has been given.

Such an interpretation of the rule allows this court to screen appeals coming from someone who has been declared vexatious to make sure such appeals do not amount to an abuse of process and to satisfy itself that there are “reasonable grounds for the proceeding” as required by section 23.1(7) of the Judicature Act.
Granting leave to vexatious litigants In Jordan v.
De Wet, 2016 ABCA 366, 2016 CarswellAlta 2225, Justice O'Ferrall had before him an application by a vexatious litigant for leave to file an appeal.

His Lordship said, at paragraphs 19–21: 19 The general test for permission to appeal under Rule 14.5 was described by Slatter JA in Thompson v Procrane Inc (Sterling Crane), 2016 ABCA 71 at paragraph 7:
(a) There is an important question of law or precedent
(b) There is a reasonable chance of success on appeal, and
(c) The delay will not unduly hinder the progress of the action or cause undue prejudice.

The test will manifest itself slightly differently, depending on the subject matter of the appeal and the overall context, but these basic principles apply to all types of applications for permission to appeal.
20 Bielby JA addressed the issue of granting leave to vexatious litigants specifically in Wong v Leung, 2012 ABCA 290, 536 AR 253.

Justice Bielby was considering section 23.1(7) of the Judicature Act, which states that the court can only grant permission to institute a proceeding or continue an existing one if it is satisfied the proceeding “is not an abuse of process and that there are reasonable grounds for proceeding”.

Her Ladyship described some of the matters that would constitute an abuse of process at paragraph 7: Justice Veit interpreted the predecessor section to 23.1(7) in Hillcox v Morrow, 175 AR 141 at para 14 as follows: …“Abuse of process” has a very wide ambit of meaning; it includes such matters as starting proceedings where issues have already been decided, and a host of other situations.

Some of these other issues include actions that cannot possibly succeed, or where no person can reasonably expect to obtain relief or where the grounds and issues have been rolled forward into subsequent actions and repeated: see Dykun v Odinshaw, 2000 ABQB 548, 267 AR 318.

21 Fundamental to both tests (the abuse of process or the reasonable grounds test) is that if the court is convinced the appeal has no chance of success, permission should not be granted. … Justice J.D.
Bruce McDonald stated the law in the same terms in E.T. v.
Calgary Catholic School District No.
1, 2017 ABCA 349, 2017 CarswellAlta 2014 at paragraphs 8–10.
In Thompson v.
International Union of Operating Engineers Local No.
995, 2017 ABCA 193, 2017 CarswellAlta 1039, Mr.
Thompson sought permission to appeal an order which had declared him to be a vexatious litigant.
The respondents contended that Rule 14.5(4) prevented the application for leave to appeal.

Madam Justice Schutz disagreed: 8 The respondents submit that Rule 14.5(4) the Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 124/2010 precludes the applicant from applying for permission to appeal the vexatious litigant order.
I disagree.

9 Rule 14.5(4) states that no appeal is allowed from an order denying a vexatious litigant leave to institute or continue proceedings; under Rule 14.5(1)(j) a person declared to be a vexatious litigant requires permission to appeal any decision.
10 Thus, a vexatious litigant order does not prohibit or deny a litigant from instituting or continuing proceedings; it simply requires that they first obtain permission.

Rule 14.5(4) expressly precludes an appeal from an order denying leave to institute or continue proceedings, but otherwise does not expressly or by necessary implication, preclude an appeal from the vexatious litigant order itself.
11 The general test for permission to appeal under Rule 14.5 is that
(a) there is an important question of law or precedent
(b) there is a reasonable chance of success on appeal, and
(c) the delay will not unduly hinder the progress of the action or cause undue prejudice: Platner v Platner, 2010 ABCA 342 at para 6.

12 In the context of an application for permission to appeal a vexatious litigant order, “the only substantive change to the general test under Rule 14.5, will be the additional burden on the applicant to show the case does not amount to an abuse of process”: Belway v Lalande-Weber, 2017 ABCA 108 at para 6.
R.
14.5(1)(a) Does Not Always Apply In Oommen v.
Alberta (Law Enforcement Review Board), 2011 ABCA 141, 2011 CarswellAlta 732, 502 A.R.
287, 24 Admin.
L.R.
(5th) 1, 45 Alta.
L.R.
287, a complaint was made against a member of the Edmonton Police Service.
The Acting Chief of the Edmonton Police Service dismissed the complaint.
The applicant appealed to the Law Enforcement Review Board which upheld the decision of the Acting Chief.
The applicant applied for leave to appeal the Board's decision.

That application was made under section 18 of the Police Act which provided that a decision of the Board could be appealed to the Court of Appeal on a question of law “with the leave of a single judge of the Court of Appeal”.
That application was denied.
The applicant then sought leave to appeal the decision of the single Court of Appeal judge.
Berger, J.A. held, at paragraph 11: 11 In my opinion, Rule 505(6) has no application where the governing statute provides for a single application for leave to appeal a tribunal's decision.
Consolidated Practice Directions See: Freyberg v.
Fletcher Challenge Oil and Gas Inc., 2006 ABCA 211 for a discussion of section 3(a)(iii) of Part J. of the Consolidated Practice Directions of the Court of Appeal.
That section says that leave must be obtained to appeal “any ruling during trial, where the appeal is brought before the trial is concluded.”

Cross appeals

paragraphs.text: (1) A respondent to an appeal may cross appeal any decision on which it could have commenced an appeal, by filing a notice of cross appeal under rule 14.11. (2) Subject to subrule (3), where an appeal has been commenced as of right or with permission, the respondent does not need permission to file a cross appeal with respect to any decision described in rule 14.5 if the cross appeal is only intended to vary the decision already under appeal. (3) Where an enactment provides that an appeal may be commenced in the Court of Appeal with permission, a respondent who wishes to cross appeal must apply for permission to cross appeal. Alta. paragraphs.text: (1) In this rule, “date of decision” means the later of (a) the date that the judgment, order or other decision being appealed is made, or (b) if reasons are given after a judgment, order or other decision being appealed is made, the date the reasons are issued. (2) An appellant must (a) file with the Registrar a notice of appeal that meets the requirements of rule 14.12 and Form AP-1, (i) within the time for commencing an appeal stated in an enactment, (ii) if the appellant is granted permission to appeal, within 10 days after the date permission is granted, or (iii) if subclauses (i) and (ii) do not apply, within one month after the date of decision, and (b) serve a filed copy of the notice of appeal on every other party to the appeal within the applicable time period mentioned in clause (a). (3) Where permission to appeal is required, an application for permission to appeal in accordance with rule 14.44 must be filed and served within the time periods mentioned in subrule (2)(a). (4) The appellant must serve a filed copy of the notice of appeal on every party to the decision that is the subject of the appeal and any person or body that these rules, an enactment or the direction of an appeal judge require to be served. (5) Appeals arising in the judicial centres of Calgary, Drumheller, Lethbridge, Medicine Hat or Red Deer must be filed at the office of the Registrar of the Court of Appeal in Calgary, and appeals arising in all other judicial centres must be filed at the office of the Registrar of the Court of Appeal in Edmonton.
