sentences.text: Commentary § 14.8:1 Rule 14.8 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta.
Reg.
Statutory Appeal Periods The court cannot extend a statutorily set appeal period.
Since the time for appeal in this case is statutory, and not contained in the Rules of Court, the provisions of the Rules of Court permitting a court to extend time for appeal have no application.
The court is without power to extend the time for appeal which has been fixed by the legislature.
W.
R.
L.R.
And Sulatycky J.A. said: A statutory time limit within which an appeal may be made also limits the time within which to apply for leave to appeal: Gell v.
Canadian Pacific Ltd., [1988] 2 S.C.R.
That decision is also authority for the conclusion that the appeal court has no inherent power to extend the time for obtaining leave to appeal.
Frost v.
Suffesick (1998), 61 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 261 (C.A.), at 263–64, per Sulatycky J.A.
Rule 14.8(1)(b) In Slawsky v.
Edmonton (City), 2019 ABCA 302, 2019 CarswellAlta 1673, a Judicial Review decision was made on January 30, 2019.
On February 15, 2009, the same chambers judge dismissed an application to reopen the costs portion of the Judicial Review decision.
Mr.
Slawsky filed a notice of appeal of the Judicial Review decision on March 4, 2019.
He took the position that the appeal period ran out on March 15, 2019.
Justice Khullar ruled that the appeal period for the Judicial Review decision expired on February 28, 2019, and that the appellant could not rely on the February 15 ruling.
Her Ladyship said [23] This argument depends on the meaning of r 14.8(1).
Under that rule, time runs from the date of the decision, which is the later of (a) the date of the decision under appeal or (b), if reasons are given later, the date the later reasons are issued.
It is implicit in r 14.8(1)(b) that the later reasons must be reasons for the decision being appealed, not reasons for some other decision.
[24] The paradigm application of r 14.8(1)(b) is when a lower court pronounces a decision with reasons “to follow”.
Under r 14.8(1)(b), the time to file a notice of appeal starts when the reasons are issued.
That makes sense because an appellant often cannot make an informed decision about whether to appeal unless she knows the reasons for the decision.
Mr.

Slawsky is arguing for a somewhat different application of r 14.8(1)(b)—the lower court pronounces a decision with full reasons and later dismisses an application to re-open that decision, also giving reasons.
Slawsky's notice of appeal purports to appeal the Judicial Review Decision.

Reduced to its essentials, he argues that the chambers judge's letter decision dated February 15, 2019 contained reasons for the costs part of the Judicial Review Decision as well as reasons for dismissing the application to re-open the Judicial Review Decision.
As Mr.
Slawsky puts it, in the February 15, 2019 reasons, the chambers judge “more fully developed” her consideration of the facts and law.
[26] I disagree.
While in some cases reasons given in a r 9.13(b) application may extend the time to appeal under r 14.8(1)(b), that is not the situation here.
The reasons given by the chambers judge in the February 15, 2019 letter decision were not reasons for the Judicial Review Decision—the costs part or any other.
They were reasons for dismissing the application to reopen the costs award.
The chambers judge declined to reopen the costs award because
(1) the award was procedurally fair since the City and the CARB made written submissions on costs before the Judicial Review Decision and
(2) the costs award did not contain a “plain and obvious error” because nothing in the Municipal Government Act, RSA 2000, c M-26 immunizes municipalities and the CARB from the normal law of costs.

[27] The reasons in the letter decision did not contribute to or change the reasons for the Judicial Review Decision; all they did was to explain why the chambers judge was not reopening the costs aspect of that decision.
It follows that that r 14.8(1)(b) has no application in this case.
[28] The time limit for appealing Judicial Review Decision fell on February 28, 2019.
It was not extended by the letter reasons of February 15, 2019 because those reasons were not reasons for the Judicial Review Decision.
Appeal period for findings of contempt In Alberta Health Services v.

Pawlowski, 2021 ABCA 344, 2021 CarswellAlta 2533, Justice Strekaf discussed when the appeal period starts to run when there has been a finding of contempt: [7] I am satisfied that the contempt finding was a “decision” within the meaning of Rule 14.8, and that the running of the appeal period with respect to that decision commenced when it was made.

In Slawsky v Edmonton (City), 2019 ABCA 302 this Court noted at paragraph 29 that, while “Rule 14.9(c) makes a single appeal of two related decisions possible in some circumstances, … it does not mean that the deadline for appealing the two decisions is the same.

Determining the deadline for filing a notice of appeal is the job of r 14.8(1), not r 14.9(c).” Generally, contempt “proceedings are bifurcated into a liability phase—where the case on liability proceeds and a defence is offered—and, if liability is established, a penalty phase.
In contempt proceedings, liability and penalty are discrete issues”: Carey v Laiken, 2015 SCC 17 at para 18, citing College of Optometrists (Ont) v SHS Optical Ltd., 2008 ONCA 685 at paras 72–75.
[8] I agree with the reasoning of the Ontario Court of Appeal in Kopaniak v MacLellan, 2002 CanLII 44919 (ON CA), 212 DLR
(4th) 309, [2002] OJ No 1642, leave to appeal to SCC refused, 2002 SCCA No 263, that the rules with respect to appeals in criminal contempt do not affect the rules for civil contempt proceedings.

The court gave several reasons for that conclusion at paragraphs 26 to 30, noting that “there is nothing in the Criminal Appeal Rules that covers contempt in a civil proceeding” and that the “Rules of Civil Procedure do apply to civil contempt proceedings”.
The same is true of Alberta's civil Rules of Court.
As the court stated at para 28, “criminal and civil contempts are very different matters”.
Enlarging Time to Appeal In Schitthelm v.
Kelemen, 2022 ABCA 334, 2022 CarswellAlta 2858, the Court of Appeal said: [6] Under R.

14.8 the appeal period runs from the pronouncement of the decision, not (as it did formerly) from the entry and service of the judgment. … [7] A litigant cannot effectively extend the time to launch an appeal by the simple expedient of asking the trial judge to reconsider the original decision: Grieve v Tasker, [1906] AC 132 at pp.
134-35 (JCPC, Nfld); Greater St Albert Roman Catholic Separate School, District No 734 v Buterman, 2014 ABQB 14 at para.
72, 570 AR 39; Molineaux v Alberta (Workers' Compensation Board, Appeals Commission), 2001 ABQB 932 at para.
Rule 13.5(2) permits the extension of an appeal period.
The test is as follows: In considering whether to extend the time for appealing or not this Division has, since 1931, followed its Judgment in Cairns v.
Cairns, [1931] 3 W.W.R.
The summary of this judgment, contained in the headnote, was approved in Ramsdell v.
Elliott and U.S.
Fidelity and Guaranty Company, [1937] 1 W.W.R.
37, by McGillivray, J.A., who had given the judgment of the majority in Cairns v.
Cairns.
This has led to some misunderstanding of the judgment apparently, not only by members of the Bar of Alberta, but by other Courts in other Provinces.

The relevant portion of the headnote reads: Where a person has recovered a judgment and the time for giving notice of appeal therefrom has expired he has a vested interest in the judgment and in the benefits which may flow from it that will not lightly be interfered with by the Courts.

Therefore an extension of time within which to give notice of appeal will not be granted as a matter of course, but a heavy burden rests on the applicant of showing cause why the indulgence of the Court should be extended to him.
It is incumbent upon him:

(1) To show that a bona-fide intention to appeal was entertained while the right to appeal existed and that the failure to appeal was by reason of some special circumstance which served to excuse or justify such failure
(2) To account for the delay and to show that the other side was not so seriously prejudiced thereby as to make it unjust, having regard to the position of both parties, to disturb the judgment
(3) To show that he has not taken the benefits of the judgment from which he is seeking to appeal
(4) To show that he would have a reasonable chance of success if allowed to prosecute the appeal.
In Cairns v.
Cairns McGillivray, J.A., after setting out the above Rules considered several conflicting English decisions.
He quoted from a Judgment of Brett, M.R., who had stated in Re Manchester Economic Building Society (1883), 24 Ch.
D.

497: I know of no other rule than this, that the Court has power to give the special leave, and exercising its judicial discretion is bound to give the special leave, if justice requires that that leave should be given.
The cases which were brought before the Court were cases in which either justice did require that the leave should be given or justice required that it should not be given.
McGillivray, J.A., then continues at p.

346: I think that the view of Brett, M.R., is to be preferred to that of James, L.J., but whatever may be said as to the conflicting decisions under the special language of the English Rule I think that it can be laid down that under our Rules this Court considers that it has a free and unfettered discretion to do what justice requires to be done between the parties having regard to the circumstances of each particular case; … This Division has relieved an applicant from its failure to comply with any of the four matters noted if there are special circumstances entitling the applicant to relief.
To simply lay down that the Court will extend the time to appeal when the justice of the situation so requires gives little help to members of the Bar in deciding how to advise a client.

This Division considers it more advantageous to require an applicant to direct his attention to the four matters specified than to lay down as a general rule that time will be extended when the justice of the situation requires.
This still leaves open what are special circumstances.
Circumstances that may occur seem myriad and I think it is quite impossible to detail them.
Reference must be made to the written judgments in which time has been or has not been extended to see what attitude the courts have taken and what may be an acceptable circumstance.
Royal Bank v.
Morin 1977, 6 A.R.
Cairns v.
Cairns, [1931] 3 W.W.R.
L.R.
69 was again applied in Petryga v.
Alberta (1980), 26 A.R.
In King v.
199 (C.A.), Ritter J.A. confirmed that the test is set forth in Cairns v.
Cairns, [1931] 3 W.W.R.
L.R.

69, and then said: The case law also indicates that even if one of the four criteria, or all four of them for that matter, are not exactly met by the proposed appellant or cross-appellant in this case, the court could still provide relief where it feels that it is appropriate.
The Court of Appeal in Bank of Montreal v.
Grotski (1992), 120 A.R.
149, at 150, confirmed that Cairns v.
Cairns sets “out the relevant considerations on an application to extend the time for appeal.” In Schulte v.

Alberta (Appeals Commission for Workers' Compensation Board), 2015 ABCA 148, Madam Justice Veldhuis said: 10 Generally all four criteria from Cairns must be satisfied, although the court may exercise its discretion to grant the extension in any event where there are unique and special circumstances and it is in the interests of justice to do so: Stoddard v Montague, 2006 ABCA 109 at para 8, 412 AR 88
Hebert v Canada, 2004 ABCA 36 at para 9.
However, the Court will not easily depart from the Cairns criteria: Seth v Walters, 2003 ABCA 160 at para 23.
In Simbajon v.
Leduc, 2015 ABCA 321, Justice O'Ferrall said at paragraph 13: “The requirements for extending the time to appeal are set out in Cairns v.
Cairns….” He then added, at paragraph 14: 14 An additional factor, not mentioned in Cairns, is the general importance of the issues on the proposed appeal.
The court may consider whether the proposed appeal is “likely to settle the law,” or whether it is of interest only to the parties: Armstrong v Armstrong, 2006 ABCA 228 at para 13, 391 AR 48.
In Attila Dogan Construction and Installation Co. v.
AMEC Americas Ltd., 2015 ABCA 206, Justice Statter said: 4 Applications to extended time to appeal are governed by the principles in Cairns v Cairns, [1931] 4 DLR 819 at pp.
826–7 (Alta SC (AD)).
It is often said that Cairns sets out a “four part test”, but that decision does not actually set out any “test”, and it mentions more than four factors:
(a) a bona fide intention to appeal held while the right to appeal existed
(b) an explanation for the failure to appeal in time that serves to excuse or justify the lateness
(c) an absence of serious prejudice such that it would not be unjust to disturb the judgment
(d) the applicant must not have taken the benefits of the judgment under appeal; and
(e) a reasonable chance of success on the appeal, which might better be described as a reasonably arguable appeal.

These factors guide the Court in exercising its discretion to extend the time to appeal, but they do not set rigid requirements, and they do not override the Court's general discretion to extend time in appropriate cases.
As noted in Cairns at p.
829 “… this Court considers that it has a free and unfettered discretion to do what justice requires to be done between the parties having regard to the circumstances of each particular case”.

5 Since there is an overriding discretion in the Court to extend the time to appeal, it is not necessary for an applicant to satisfy all components of the Cairns test: Stoddard v Montague, 2006 ABCA 109 at para.
It is more accurate to say that if the applicant does satisfy all the components of the Cairns test, it is highly likely that an extension will be granted.
Nevertheless, the appropriate approach is to address the Cairns factors first: Royal Bank of Canada v Morin (1977), 6 AR 341 at para.
8, 4 Alta LR (2d) 127 (App Div).
However, in the end the Cairns factors and the surrounding circumstances must be considered and weighed collectively in deciding whether an extension of time is warranted. ….
8 It is true that Cairns contemplates “some very special circumstance which serves to excuse or justify” the late appeal.
Cairns, however, was a custody dispute engaging the interests of a child: finality was of prime importance, and the procedural history was unsatisfactory.
While some acceptable explanation for the lateness is required, the reason, considered in isolation, need not be “very special”.
The source of the error must be weighed with all of the other factors, such as the length of the delay, prejudice from granting or denying the application, and all the other relevant considerations.

9 In many cases of a short delay of a day or two, weighing the various components of the Cairns test will result in the Court exercising its discretion to grant an extension: RIC New Brunswick Inc. v Telecommunications Research Laboratories, 2010 ABCA 75 at para.
Justice Schutz summarized the factors to be considered on an application to extend the time to appeal in Murphy v.
Haworth, 2016 ABCA 219, 2016 CarswellAlta 1376: 5 The following factors guide the court's discretion to extend time to appeal:
(a) a bona fide intention to appeal held while the right to appeal existed
(b) an explanation for the failure to appeal in time that serves to excuse or justify the lateness
(c) an absence of serious prejudice such that it would not be unjust to disturb the judgment
(d) the applicant must not have taken the benefits of the judgment under appeal; and

(e) a reasonable chance of success on the appeal, which might better be described as a reasonably arguable appeal. * (Attila Dogan Construction and Installation Co v AMEC Americas Ltd, 2015 ABCA 206 at para 4
Cairns v Cairns[1931] 4 DLR 819 at 826-827, 26 Alta LR 69 (SC(AD))

Sohal v Brar, 1998 ABCA 375, 223 AR 141 at para 1) 6 In addition to the Cairns factors, this court may consider whether the proposed appeal is “likely to settle the law” or whether it is of interest only to the parties: Simbajohn v Leduc, 2015 ABCA 321 at para 14.
7 Finally, because this court has an overriding discretion to extend time to appeal, it is not necessary for a successful applicant to satisfy all the components of the Cairns test.
This court may exercise this discretion “to do what justice requires to be done between the parties having regard to the circumstances of each particular case”: Cairns at 829.
In Rai v.
Alberta (Labour Relations Board), 2019 ABCA 497, 2019 CarswellAlta 2684, Justice J.D.

Bruce McDonald said: [16] The test to be considered in an application to extend the time for filing a Notice of Appeal is derived from this Court's decision in Cairns v Cairns, 1931 CanLII 471 (AB CA), [1931] 4 DLR 819 (Alta SC AD), and as more recently restated in Travis v D&J Overhead Doors Ltd, 2016 ABCA 319 at para 6–11.
[17] The test may be stated as follows.
First, did the applicant form an intention to appeal while the right of appeal existed?
Second, has the applicant provided an explanation for the failure to file a timely appeal?
Third, if so, does his explanation constitute “some very special circumstance which serves to excuse or justify such failure”?
Fourth, has the applicant demonstrated that the delay has not “so seriously prejudiced the respondent as to make it unjust” to grant a time extension?
Fifth, has the applicant not taken the benefits of the judgment?
Sixth, it falls on the applicant to convince the court that “he had a reasonable chance of success if allowed to commence and prosecute the appeal”.
That restated test was quoted with approval in Wolfe v.
Morrisseau, 2021 ABCA 205, 2021 CarswellAlta 1328 at para.
10, and in Kuzik v.
Hagel, 2021 ABCA 241, 2021 CarswellAlta 1577, 58 R.F.L.
(8th) 6 at para.
With respect to assessing the merits of the proposed appeal, Justice Rowbotham said at paragraph 6 of Alberta Treasury Branches v.
Conserve Oil 1st Corp., 2016 ABCA 87, 2016 CarswellAlta 548: 6 Both the extension of time to appeal and the leave applications require an assessment of the merits of the appeal.
Under the Cairns[1931] 3 W.W.R.

335 test to extend the time to appeal, the applicant must establish that the appeal has a reasonable chance of success if allowed to proceed: Cairns v Cairns, [1931] 4 DLR 819 (Alta SC (AD)), 1931 3 WWR 335.

To satisfy this requirement, the applicant must only show that there is a “reasonable chance of success, not certainty or even likely victory” and that the appeal is not hopeless: Kerr v Robert Mathew Investments Inc., 2008 ABCA 193 at para 5, 433 AR 251.
However, the burden is higher where the decision of the lower court is subject to a deferential standard of appellate review: Berro v Berro, 2001 ABCA 157 at para 17, 93 Alta LR (3d) 230.

The application for leave to appeal requires that the appeal be prima facie meritorious, or not frivolous: Simonelli v Macklin, 2003 ABCA 47 at para 28, 320 AR 330; Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, RSC 1985, c B-3 (“BIA”), s 193(e).
In Pe Ben Oilfield Services v.
WCB, 2018 ABCA 139, 2018 CarswellAlta 681, Justice J.D.
Bruce McDonald discussed the “merits of the appeal” requirement, and noted that the stringency of the requirement depends on the standard of review which will be applied in the proposed appeal.
His Lordship said: 23 The applicant seeks to appeal matters of statutory interpretation which would be reviewed on a standard of correctness.
Therefore the burden of a reasonable prospect of success is not as high as an appeal subject to a deferential standard of review: Conserve Oil 1st Corp at para 6.
Therefore given the modest requirement of success “not certainty or even likely victory” and that the appeal is not hopeless, I find that the applicant has met this requirement as well.
Under these circumstances, I will refrain from making any further comment on the merits.

With respect to the intent to appeal and extending the time to appeal when another party has filed a timely notice of appeal, the Court of Appeal said this: Ordinarily the Court of Appeal will not extend time to appeal where there was no intent in time to appeal … … In our view, the need to form an intent to appeal in time is much watered down where another member of the same class of creditors did appeal in time and where, had the appeal prevailed, the result would have accrued to benefit all the members of that class … It is admitted that there is no prejudice to the respondent, as it is no harder to respond to an appeal by one secured creditor than by another.
Weldwood of Canada Ltd. v.
Alberta Export Mills Corp.
L.R.
(3d) 377 (C.A.), at 378, per Côté J.A.
In Kure v.
Kure, 2017 ABCA 215, 2017 CarswellAlta 1166, Justice Strekaf had before her an application to restore an appeal.
Her Ladyship, in considering the reason for the delay which resulted in the appeal being struck, said, at paragraph 11: 11 Waiting for an order is not a sufficient reason to justify a delay.

The law is clear that the order takes effect from the time that it is granted and if a party is unsure of which order is going to be filed but has an a genuine intention to appeal, or if one form of the order is preferred over the other, then that notice of appeal should have been filed and could always be abandoned later.
This is not a sufficient excuse to justify not filing an appeal within the designated appeal period.
In Kuzik v.
Hagel, 2021 ABCA 241, 2021 CarswellAlta 1577, 58 R.F.L.
(8th) 6, the Court commented on the sufficiency of an explanation (that the applicant was mistaken as to the law) given for the failure to file the notice of appeal on time.

The Court said: [11] In his affidavit sworn May 12, 2021, at paragraphs 10-11, Mr Kuzik states that on February 25, 2021, he was emailed the draft Matrimonial Property Judgment, but did not agree with it and did not sign it.
On March 18, 2021, he received the Matrimonial Property Judgment signed by the Justice, but “without my signature on it”.

Mr Kuzik states he “was under the mistaken impression that I had 30 days from the receipt of the Matrimonial Property [Judgment] to file the Appeal, being April 18, 2021”. “[A] mistaken view of the law or procedure is itself not enough excuse, especially in the absence of evidence of due diligence”: Real Life Homes & Investments Ltd v Wert Homes and Investments Ltd, 2012 ABCA 3 at para 8.

[12]“There also has to be sufficient evidence of such mistaken understanding of the applicable rule or law”: Fromhold v Lacombe (County of), 2019 ABCA 472 at para 12, citing Schulte v Alberta (Appeals Commission for Workers' Compensation Board), 2015 ABCA 148 at para 13. … However, in Macdonald v.
King, 2021 ABCA 258, 2021 CarswellAlta 1666, Justice Slatter noted that there is no absolute rule against finding that a misunderstanding of the Rules is a sufficient explanation.

His Lordship said: [7] The respondent argues that misinterpreting the effect of the Rules of Court or overlooking a rule, has not been accepted as a sufficient explanation for late filing, citing Adderley v 1400467 Alberta Ltd., 2014 ABCA 291 at para.
12 and Schulte v Alberta (Workers' Compensation Appeals Commission), 2015 ABCA 148 at para.
There is in fact no such absolute rule.
As pointed out in Attila Dogan at para.
7, a significant number of successful applications to extend the time to appeal involved errors of this type.
There is no principled reason why “human error” should not be sufficient to explain an inadvertent late filing.

Lawyers may be expected to have superior knowledge about matters of procedure, but that does not mean that they are perfect, nor do the Rules of Court expect that lawyers will never make mistakes: compare R.
1.5 on non-compliance and the remedies for it.
There is also no principled reason to try and draw a distinction between “mistakes of fact” and “mistakes of law”.
Both can be equally effective in creating procedural noncompliance.
Finally, it must be remembered that the Court of Appeal has unfettered discretion to extend the time to appeal when it considers it appropriate to do so.
In Higdon v.
Smoky Lake General & Auxiliary Hospital & Nursing Home District 73 (1983), 29 Alta.
L.R.
(2d) 215, the Court of Appeal, speaking through McGillivray C.J.A., said, at p.
219: We are all of the opinion that the court does have an unfettered discretion to extend the time for appealing, notwithstanding that one of the usual requirements as stated in Cairns v.
Cairns has not been met… We think that these observations [those reproduced above from Royal Bank v.
Morin] indicate that the court should in every case consider the requirements set out in Cairns v.
Cairns… but that the court does retain the unfettered discretion to extend the time for appealing if the justice of the situation so requires.
This principle was applied in Bareau v.
University of Alberta (1995), 35 Alta.
L.R.
414–15, a decision of Madam Justice Phillips.
The principle was confirmed by Ritter J.A. in Buckley v.
Buckley (2004), 357 A.R.
199 where his Lordship said: “Exceptionally, even if the (sic) or more of these four requirements are not met the court may extend time where the interests of justice so dictate. …” In Armstrong v.
Armstrong (2006), 60 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 21 (C.A.), the Chambers judge reduced a father's access times to his child.
The father did not file an appeal within the specified time, and applied for an extension of the appeal period.
Côté J.A., sitting alone, heard the application, and provided the following review of the applicable law: (1) Reasonable chance of success (at pp.
23–24) According to many authorities from Alberta and elsewhere, one branch of the test for extending time to appeal is “a reasonable chance of success” on the merits of the proposed appeal.
See Cairns v.
Cairns, [1931] 3 W.W.R.
335 (Alta.
Though some English authorities take the view that the answer to this question must be a simple yes or no, Canadian authorities tend to disagree, and often seem to weigh the merits to some extent.
A number of Alberta decisions have refused to extend time on the grounds that the apparent merits of the appeal were too weak, even if it was not absolutely hopeless or frivolous: Horrey v.
Litterst (1995), 32 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 40 (Alta.
C.A.), 44 (para.
12) (one J.A.); Royal Bank v.
144 (Alta.
On access and child maintenance appeals, see Stewart v.
Stewart (1990), 112 A.R.
137 (Alta.
C.A.); Berro v.
C.A.); and Little v.
Little (1998), 228 A.R.
(2) Does the appeal raise issues of general importance?
25) In other areas of procedure, such as motions for leave to appeal, an important consideration is often law-making vs. error-correcting.
In other words, is the proposed suit or appeal of value to the community because it is likely to settle the law, or is it of interest only to these parties?
That factor is not mentioned in Cairns v.
Cairns, supra.
But it is given weight in some other Canadian cases on extending time to appeal.
One of them is a decision of a panel of our Court: Hill v.
Barwis (1908), 1 Alta.
L.R.
274 (Alta.
That was an important consideration in refusing to extend time there.
I cannot find that that case has ever been overruled.
The British Columbia Court of Appeal appears to have held the same view in Guglielmucci v.
Makowichuk (1995), 71 B.C.A.C.
(3) Intent to appeal (p.
25) Though it is often said in Alberta that the test for extending time to appeal has four parts, in fact the “first” part has two distinct subparts: see Cairns v.
Cairns, supra, at 343.
The first subpart is a bona fide intention to appeal which was held before the time to appeal expired ….
(4) Reason for missing the deadline (p.
25) The second subpart of the first test is “some very special circumstance which serves to excuse or justify” the failure to appeal in time: Cairns v.
Cairns, supra, at p.
(5) The delay (p.
26) The “second” branch of the test for extending time to appeal also has two subparts.
The first subpart is to account for the delay: Cairns v.
Cairns, supra, at 344.
(I am not sure whether that somewhat duplicates an earlier branch).
(6) Prejudice to the respondent (p.
26) The second subpart of the “second” branch of the test is to show that the respondent has not been seriously prejudiced by the delay so as to make it unjust to extend the time: Cairns v.
Cairns, supra, at 344.
Côté J.A. then noted that the parties entered into negotiations about the wording of the formal order and about matters not covered by the chambers order.
On the point of prejudice arising from the respondent negotiating without knowing that an appeal was to be launched, his Lordship said at p.
28: In any event, the British Columbia Court of Appeal has held that whether the appellant gave notice to the respondent of his intent to appeal is a relevant point to weigh: see C.
C.
That factor was also given some weight by our Court in Little v.
Little, supra (para.
In many reported cases where time to appeal was extended, the appellant did informally tell the respondent of the intended appeal before the time expired.
Some of the cases seem to rely on that fact.
I cannot think of a reason why a court should ignore that factor, even if such notice is not a mandatory precondition for time extension.
Finally, Côté J.A. noted that prejudice can go beyond the process of litigation.
At p.
29, he discussed that by way of an example from the facts before him.
His Lordship said: Relevant prejudice is not limited to the mechanics of litigation.
Some involves the parties' lives.
This litigation is supposed to be for the benefit of the daughter, not her parents.
Since a year will have elapsed by then, I presume that the daughter will start school at the beginning of September.
The law requires her to do so, as she will then be 6 years and 3 months old.
It will be very inconvenient for her and her mother (the respondent) to pick a school and begin to attend it, without knowing what the custody and access arrangements are.
That concern is not hypothetical; the would-be appellant wants the child to attend a specific school not acceptable to the respondent mother, and the formal order rejects that request (para.
If the appeal proceeds, no decision is possible on that or any other issue before the second week in September.
Spring and summer are sensitive seasons for delays, in child custody cases.
So the delay in appealing likely prejudiced the respondent mother, and the daughter.
(7) Taking the benefits of the Order (pp.
29-30) I have already discussed negotiating without revealing intent to appeal later (in Part H).
The other traditional test for extending time to appeal is whether the would-be appellant has taken the fruits of the judgment.
See Cairns v.
Cairns, supra, at p.
344; Horrey v.
Litterst, supra at 44-45 (para.
Menear (2002), 155 O.A.C.
13 (Ont.
C.A.), 19 (para.
The respondent's counsel argues that the would-be appellant father has; he is now on holidays with his daughter, under a type of access ordered by the impugned order and not earlier.
That is not in any affidavit, though the newly-entered order does give him a three-week summer access with his daughter.
The previous provisions in the divorce judgment had made that one week.
I hesitate to apply that rule about taking the fruits, to merely exercising custody or access granted by the order to be appealed.
It is true that this rule forbids blowing hot and cold: one must elect to accept (claim under) or reject (appeal) the order.
But there is no rule against blowing hot and hotter (taking and seeking more of the same).
Cf. an expropriation case, Petryga v.
Alberta (1980), 26 A.R.
290 (Alta.
C.A.), 295 (para.
With respect to the reason that party failed to file the Notice of Appeal within the stipulated time, Justice Veldhuis said in Schulte v.

Alberta (Appeals Commission for Workers' Compensation Board), 2015 ABCA 148: 14 Even if there was some evidence of confusion on the applicant's part, misunderstanding a pertinent rule or procedure does not constitute a special circumstance that reasonably explains a delay in filing, particularly in the absence of due diligence: Adderley v 1400467 Alberta Ltd, 2014 ABCA 291 at paras 10–12, 580 AR 319
Real Life Homes & Investments Ltd v Wert Homes and Investments Ltd, 2012 ABCA 3 at para 8.
However, in Attila Dogan Construction and Installation Co. v.

AMEC Americas Ltd., 2015 ABCA 257, Justice Slatter said: 4 The respondents argue specifically that recent decisions have held that errors by counsel, particularly misunderstanding an applicable rule, do not qualify as a sufficient justification for extending the time to appeal under the Cairns test.
In this case, the error of counsel in calculating the appeal period falls in that category.
The respondents rely on Schulte v Alberta (Workers' Compensation Appeals Commission), 2015 ABCA 148 at para.
14, but that decision involved a self-represented appellant, and did not say that “errors by counsel” are a never a sufficient explanation.

Further, the Schulte decision involved a lengthy delay, with the Court holding: “While a brief delay might be understood, he waited for nearly two and a half years”, and “The applicant has not provided any explanation or evidence as to why he thought that he did not have to file the Notice to Appeal in time.” The Schulte reasons must be read in the factual context that generated them.

5 Schulte did suggest in obiter that “misunderstanding a pertinent rule or procedure does not constitute a special circumstance that reasonably explains a delay in filing, particularly in the absence of due diligence”.
Schulte cited Adderley v 1400467 Alberta Ltd., 2014 ABCA 291 at paras 10–12, 580 AR 319 and Real Life Homes & Investments Ltd. v Wert Homes and Investments Ltd., 2012 ABCA 3 at para 8 in support.
6 Adderley must also be read in its factual context.

There the error was by a student-at-law, and the explanation was not sufficient under the Cairns test “not only because the student missed the deadline, but also because no-one responsible for carriage of the file ensured that this important step, in complex and expensive litigation, actually occurred” (emphasis in original).
Real Life Homes also involved a self-represented applicant.
The application was unsuccessful due to the absence of evidence of a reasonable explanation for the delay, no due diligence, and a lack of merit in the proposed appeal.
Neither decision supports the categorical proposition that mistakes over procedural requirements are never a sufficient explanation under the Cairns test.

7 There are undoubtedly cases where an error by counsel, or a misunderstanding of the pertinent rule, was found not to be a sufficient excuse in the particular context, but that does not mean that there is a fixed rule to that effect.
The various factors in the Cairns test must be weighed together, and whether to permit a late appeal is ultimately in the discretion of the Court: Cairns at p.
829; Stoddard v Montague, 2006 ABCA 109 at para.

Because there is an overriding discretion to permit a late appeal even if the Cairns test is not met, it does not advance the analysis to say that certain explanations can “never” be acceptable under that test.
The Court could theoretically grant an extension even if none of the Cairns factors were met.
8 There are numerous cases where an error by counsel or a misunderstanding of the procedural requirements did not preclude a late appeal.
For example, in Hudson v Bower (sub nom.
Shewchuk, Re) (1968), 67 WWR 564 at pp.
564-5, 1 DLR (3d) 288 (Alta SC (App Div)) it was held: 2 On the opening of the appeal, objection was taken that the notice of appeal had been given out of time.

The appellant applied for an extension of time within which to appeal and, on that application, it was made to appear that the solicitors for the appellant had mistakenly believed that the Rule which extends the time for filing pleadings during vacation also applied to the filing of notices of appeal.

Under an earlier English Rule, mistake or misunderstanding by a solicitor or counsel of the meaning of the Rules was not such a special circumstance as would induce the Court to give the leave which is required to extend the time.
That was under a Rule that required a special application for that purpose.
Our Rule, as well as later English Rules, do not require a special application and the requirements for an order under the Rule are not as stringent.
While solicitors are presumed to know the proper interpretation of the Rules of Court, experience has shown that this presumption is often not well founded.
In the present case the delay was short and no prejudice was shown, and the appellant having shown a reasonable chance of success on the appeal, we have accordingly extended the time for appeal.
To the same effect are: Royal Bank of Canada v Morin (1977), 6 AR 341 at para.
17, 4 Alta LR (2d) 127 (App Div); L.C. v Alberta, 2009 ABCA 77 at para.
8, 448 AR 293; Jackson v Canadian National Railway Co., 2015 ABCA 89 at para.
7; and Phoenix Land Ventures Ltd. v FIC Real Estate Fund Ltd., 2015 ABCA 245 at paras.
Hudson and Royal Bank are decisions of full panels of the Court, not just single judges.
Affidavits sworn by legal assistants—Unacceptable Except for Non-controversial Matters In Tole v.
Lucki (Guardian ad litem of), 2017 ABCA 79, 2017 CarswellAlta 336, Justice Strekaf had before her an application to file a notice of appeal outside the permitted period.
In opposition to the application, an affidavit sworn by a legal assistant of the respondents's lawyer was filed.

Her Ladyship said: 8 The respondent's lawyer's legal assistant swore an affidavit to the effect that she was advised by the lawyer and verily believed that related actions “have stalled partially as a result of the delay”.
9 The swearing of an affidavit by a legal assistant is unacceptable other than for noncontroversial matters.
While this practice has been criticized by the court on numerous occasions, it still occurs too often: Chernetz v Eagle Copters Ltd, 2002 ABQB 986 at para 12
Calf Robe v Canada, 2006 ABQB 652 at paras 10-11
Desoto Resources Limited v Encana Corporation, 2009 ABQB 512 at para 12.
In this case, the legal assistant is at least two steps away from the party who is said to have been prejudiced by the delay.

The party asserting prejudice (rather than its counsel and much less its counsel's assistant) should file an affidavit outlining the nature and extent of the prejudice claimed and be available to be cross-examined on the affidavit.
In Canada (Attorney General) v.
Andronyk, 2017 ABCA 139, 2017 CarswellAlta 786, 55 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 356, Justice Watson discussed an instance which qualified as one of the “noncontroversial matters” referred to by Justice Strekaf.
At paragraphs 19–21, his Lordship said: [19] The second affidavit was of Mark Stanicki, a legal assistant with Justice Canada, who reported to counsel for the Attorney General.
His affidavit essentially annexed the relevant court records and the Minister's surrender order relating to the applicant.
He also provided information that the applicant had not complied with the requirements as to filing and serving on that office of a factum on the application for judicial review.

[20] On this topic, I would observe that I do not part company with the concern expressed in the decision of Strekaf JA in Tole v Lucki, 2017 ABCA 79 at para 9, [2017] AJ No 184 (QL) about potential misuses of affidavits of legal assistants that are essentially hearsay in content.
To me, however, this affidavit contains the sort of non-controversial information which is a recognized exception in Tole.

[21] Moreover, it is helpful to assemble court records and other procedural fact evidence in an affidavit like this rather than commit a judge to ferret through court records to ascertain the same contextual circumstances.

Court records are, prima facie, admissible in their own right as well as under the Canada Evidence Act, both for procedural fact purposes and for adjudicative fact purposes, such as proof of breach of recognizance, subject to adjudicative fairness considerations: see R v Tatomir, 1989 ABCA 233, 99 AR 188, leave denied [1989] SCCA No 448 (SCC No 21713)
R v West, 2011 BCCA 109 at paras 3–19, [2011] BCJ No 583 (QL)
R v Jerace, 2016 ABCA 70 at paras 7-8, [2016] AJ No 239 (QL) leave denied
(2016) [2016] SCCA No 342 (QL) (SCC No 37150); R v Caesar, 2016 ONCA 599, 339 CCC
(3d) 354; and compare Kon Construction Ltd v Terranova Developments Ltd, 2015 ABCA 249 at paras 13–15, 387 DLR
(4th) 623 as to routinely (and electronically) recorded evidence.
In Remington Development Corporation v.
Enmax Power Corporation, 2019 ABQB 754, 2019 CarswellAlta 2070 (Master), Master Robertson had before him an application to amend a statement of claim.
The evidence in support of the application was submitted by way of an affidavit sworn by a legal assistant.
The learned Master said: [15] As to the sufficiency of the evidence, in my view it was appropriate, although not necessarily the best practice, to have a legal assistant swear the affidavit.
It simply puts before the Court the agreement, and subsequent decisions so as to sketch out the history to give a background to the application for the amendment.
This kind of affidavit is admissible: Canada (Attorney General) v Andronyk, 2017 ABCA 139 at para.
[16] The evidence it put forth in this affidavit was not in controversy, and Enmax does not suggest that there is any important evidence not there.
It argues that it lost the opportunity to cross-examine a witness who had real knowledge of the case.
It does not say what it might have been able to bring out in a cross-examination.

Since the evidence put forward is enough to properly found the application to amend, and the evidence put forward is not in controversy, I see nothing wrong with providing an affidavit from a legal assistant.
